body.title: living-cryptography: state the original design alongside the research question
body.body:
## What changes
README and docs/README: in the original design a specialised AI authenticates each request, the scheme aims to resist quantum computation, and the network behaves like a hydra — a failed attempt reconfigures the encryption, an attack makes it stronger, and authentication work also helps process and move data. The research question and its evaluation requirements stay.

## Why
Restores part of the founder's original design that earlier edits had left out (sweep of 2026-10-05). Founder's instruction: "pode atualizar tudo".

body.title: Authenticated channels for the veto chain; English-only documentation
body.body:
Alignment pass across the `draykerdk` organization, on the branch `alinhamento/2026-09` in every affected repository.

## Changes

- docs: authenticated channels for the veto chain; English only

## Across the organization

- Governance corrected: PAP is Projects & Applications, DFMP is the DFM proposal process, the founding account is `Hyadhuad`, and the governance horizon runs from the founding Embassy through the DAF into PAP.
- The veto chain specified in UID: signed, hash-linked vetoes that carry their real grounds even when anonymous; vetoes weighed by grounds, not counted; one veto with grounds beyond the decision's scope can lead to an adjustment after advanced triage.
- Direction states 2033 as the objective, measured by what works rather than by the date.
- Intelligence is a partner, never the master.
- English is the canonical documentation language.
- Documentation states its own claims and does not cite outside books as authority.

Documentation only. Nothing here claims an implemented system.

Supersedes #4, closed when the branch was renamed.

body.title: Write a threat model for re-encryption on failed authentication
body.body:
## What is delivered
A threat model for the design where a failed authentication changes the cryptographic scheme: what it defends against, what it does not, and what it costs.

## Why it is needed
The claim is strong — that repeating a brute-force attempt stops paying off, and that the system gets stronger under attack. A claim that strong needs an adversary written down next to it.

## Where to start
Useful attacks to reason about: an adversary who fails deliberately to force re-encryption; the cost of re-encryption to legitimate holders of the data; what happens to data in flight during a scheme change; and whether an attacker can distinguish schemes.

A well-argued "this does not hold under X" is as valuable as a defence of the design.
## Prior material

Drayker has earlier work on this subject in its own knowledge base — drafts, mostly in Portuguese, written before the public repositories took their current shape. It is not published yet. If you take this function, say so in the thread and the relevant material will be published alongside it, so you are consolidating and arguing with existing thinking rather than starting from a blank page.

---
This is an open function: small enough for one person to finish, defined enough that the result composes with the rest. Claim it in this thread before starting so two people do not carry the same function, and deliver through a pull request to `master`. It appears on the board at https://drayker.org/#org/fn

body.title: Specify the uPOW: inputs, cost and verification
body.body:
## What is delivered
A specification of the unit of proof-of-work a requester must run: what it takes as input, how its cost is set, how the distributed system verifies it, and how the split between authentication work and network work is decided.

## Why it is needed
The uPOW is the mechanism the whole security model rests on, and what is published is currently one paragraph of prose. Nothing about it can be reviewed, implemented or attacked on paper in its present form.

## Where to start
The README describes the intent. The hard questions are the useful ones: who chooses the difficulty, what stops it from being a denial-of-service against legitimate users, and what exactly the network gets back for the work spent.
## Prior material

Drayker has earlier work on this subject in its own knowledge base — drafts, mostly in Portuguese, written before the public repositories took their current shape. It is not published yet.
